notes: Detailed Silber J judgment on tenant relocation; natural justice breach clearly identified as ground for quashing.

enrichment.short_title: Market traders' judicial review succeeds where council failed to allow comment on relocation selection material
key_facts: Hounslow Council decided to replace the Western International Market at Southall with a smaller new market about two-thirds of its size, requiring selection among existing tenants.
A Relocation Committee assessed tenants on use, financial standing and rent payment record but tenants were not shown adverse information relied on against them before decisions were made.
Unsuccessful applicants including A1 Veg and the Agnello claimants challenged refusals of units in the new market by judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the London Borough of Hounslow's decisions refusing market traders units in the proposed new Western International Market.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; applications succeeded; relocation allocation decisions quashed for failure to afford tenants an opportunity to comment on information used against them.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority selects tenants for relocation to a new public market using comparative evaluation of adverse material about individual applicants, procedural fairness requires that each applicant be given a reasonable opportunity to comment on that information before the decision is made; failure to do so is a breach of natural justice warranting quashing even if other Wednesbury or reasons challenges fail.
legal_issues: Whether the council's tenant selection decision was amenable to judicial review
Whether delay barred the claims
Whether the council breached natural justice by failing to allow tenants to comment on adverse selection material
Whether the decision was Wednesbury unreasonable or inadequately reasoned

notes: Arkin v Borchard costs judgment (No.3) establishing Part 20 costs principles after impecunious claimant.

enrichment.short_title: Part 20 defendants recover costs from joining defendant despite impecunious claimant in shipping cartel litigation
key_facts: After a 49-day trial Mr Arkin's EC competition claim against shipping conference defendants including Borchard failed and substantial costs orders were made against the impecunious claimant.
Borchard had joined Zim and other Part 20 defendants; the main claim failed so Borchard's Part 20 claim against them also failed, but those defendants sought their costs from Borchard.
Mr Arkin could not satisfy costs orders and no section 51(3) order had been made against his litigation funder MPC.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs application following trial in long-running shipping conference litigation (Arkin v Borchard, No.3) concerning liability for Part 20 defendants' costs.
enrichment.outcome: Part 20 defendants entitled to costs orders against Borchard (Zim 90% and DAC Part 20 defendants 80%, mirroring main action reductions); no cut-through order against Mr Arkin and no aggregated expert-costs sharing order.
enrichment.ratio: Part 20 proceedings are separate from the main action and costs normally follow the event in those proceedings; the claimant's impecuniosity in the main action is not ordinarily a sufficient reason to depart from that rule and impose on a successful Part 20 defendant the burden of irrecoverable costs, save in exceptional cases where Part 20 issues are co-extensive with the main claim and injustice would otherwise be extreme.
legal_issues: Whether Borchard should pay Part 20 defendants' costs or those costs should be routed to the impecunious claimant
Whether a Sanderson or Bullock-style cut-through costs order was appropriate
Whether expert evidence costs should be shared rateably among successful defendants
How Johnson v Ribbins and Bankamerica Finance v Nock apply to Part 20 costs

notes: Holman J reflective judgment after care proceedings withdrawn following reversed medical expert evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Care proceedings withdrawn after joint examination showed colposcopic photographs had misled experts on alleged sexual abuse
key_facts: A local authority commenced care proceedings after medical examinations of a young girl T suggested hymenal trauma consistent with penetrative sexual abuse by her stepfather.
The father was twice required to leave the family home and the children were removed to foster care while expert paediatric evidence consistently supported abuse findings.
On joint examination in June 2003 Drs Evans and Sunderland found no evidence of abuse, concluded earlier photographs were unreliable, and the local authority withdrew its care applications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Permission granted to local authority to withdraw care order applications; Holman J published a non-adjudicatory judgment summarising the history for professional learning after a fresh hearing directed by the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Local authority permitted to withdraw care proceedings; all proceedings ended; no findings made by Holman J but the medical evidence no longer supported a finding of sexual abuse.
enrichment.ratio: This judgment does not decide contested issues but records that misleading colposcopic still photography and incomplete examination technique can produce grave misreadings in alleged child sexual abuse cases, reinforcing that clinical examination remains the gold standard and repeat examination may be necessary to avoid miscarriage of justice.
legal_issues: Whether care proceedings should be withdrawn in light of reversed expert medical evidence
Reliability of colposcopic photography in paediatric forensic sexual abuse examinations
Appropriate use of repeat intimate examination where photographic and note evidence conflict

notes: Large TCC trial on solicitors' negligence counterclaim; professional negligence defence succeeded.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors not liable for student housing delay losses where GC/Works contract limited remedy to liquidated damages
key_facts: Masons acted for W D King on a Bath student accommodation development using a GC/Works/1 building contract with Jarvis as contractor and PGBL as special purpose vehicle employer.

After delay and an unsuccessful adjudication against Jarvis, WDK/PGBL counterclaimed alleging Masons should have drafted the contract to allow unliquidated damages for breach of Condition 38 acceleration instructions.
Masons sued for unpaid fees of £37,093; more than £250,000 had already been paid for extensive drafting and advisory work.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court on Masons' claim for unpaid fees and WDK/PGBL's professional negligence counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Counterclaim failed: no retainer or duty of care owed to PGBL; building contract did not permit unliquidated damages for Condition 38 breach; Masons not in breach of duty to WDK; causation not established.
enrichment.ratio: Under GC/Works/1 a failure to comply with a Condition 38 acceleration instruction does not give rise to a separate claim for unliquidated damages where liquidated damages under Condition 55 are the contractual remedy for late completion; a solicitor retained by the project sponsor owes no duty of care to an SPV employer merely because contract documents name that vehicle.
legal_issues: Whether Masons' retainer was with WDK or PGBL
Whether Masons owed PGBL a concurrent duty of care in negligence
Whether the building contract allowed unliquidated damages for breach of Condition 38
Whether any breach of duty caused WDK/PGBL's lost opportunity to recover delay losses from Jarvis

notes: Leading Court of Appeal judgment on adoption agency negligence and information disclosure duties.

enrichment.short_title: Adoption agency liable only for failing to communicate decided disclosure material, not for content of reports
key_facts: Essex County Council placed siblings William and Kate with prospective adopters without ensuring they received full medical reports describing William's serious behavioural problems.
After adoption William's violent behaviour caused psychiatric and physical injury to the adoptive parents, who claimed they would not have accepted placement had they been fully informed.
Buckley J held the authority liable but limited recoverable loss to the period before adoption orders were made.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from Buckley J's trial judgment on negligence by a local authority adoption agency in pre-placement information disclosure.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; local authority remained liable but on narrower grounds—breach of duty to communicate information the agency had decided to disclose, not breach in deciding what to disclose or compiling reports; damages limited to pre-adoption period upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An adoption agency owes prospective adopters no general duty of care in deciding what information to disclose or in compiling Form E and medical reports, but once it decides particular information should be given there is a duty to take reasonable steps to ensure it is communicated; liability for psychiatric injury may follow Page v Smith where physical injury was foreseeable.

Whether breach of Adoption Agencies Regulations 1983 reg 12 gives rise to private law liability
Whether failure to provide medical reports before placement caused the adopters to accept the children

enrichment.short_title: Broker ordered to pay 90% of own costs after unauthorised alteration of warranty fax triggered reinsurance dispute
key_facts: Groupama sued OP Re on a marine personal accident quota share treaty; OP Re relied on a June 1998 fax confirming no losses on the programme.
Aon, as broker, had removed the words 'to LDG' from a draft fax approved by the underwriter Smart, materially changing the warranty representation.
Morison J held OP Re's avoidance defence failed but ordered Aon to bear its own costs because its alteration caused the litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against Morison J's costs order following trial in the Commercial Court on a reinsurance treaty claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; OP Re ordered to pay Aon 90% of its costs of the action; 10% of Aon's costs disallowed reflecting its unauthorised fax alteration.
enrichment.ratio: Under CPR 44.3(4)(a) a court may have regard to a party's conduct before proceedings when making costs orders; however depriving a successful joined defendant of all costs for pre-litigation conduct that was not dishonest and where the unsuccessful party pursued bad interpretive points to trial is a disproportionate exercise of discretion warranting appellate intervention.

notes: False imprisonment appeal concerning blanket arrests of CCTV wardens; Brooke LJ expressed unease but appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Police arrests of CCTV wardens lawful despite opportunity-only suspicion after tampered evidence tapes
key_facts: Five council CCTV wardens and a colleague were arrested over four days on suspicion of perverting the course of justice after spot and multiplex tapes of a car crime incident were tampered with.
Police narrowed suspects to six staff with opportunity to interfere but could not pinpoint timing because they doubted the spot tape was original.
All arrested were innocent; Starbuck later admitted inadvertently recording over the spot tape; multiplex tampering remained unresolved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against HHJ Hewitt's dismissal of claims for wrongful arrest and false imprisonment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; arrests held lawful on reasonable suspicion and Wednesbury-compliant discretion.
enrichment.ratio: Opportunity can amount to reasonable grounds for suspicion under PACE s 24(6) where police have narrowed suspects to a small irreducible group after reasonable inquiry; arrest for questioning to obtain a confession is a proper purpose under Holgate-Mohammed, and Article 5 does not require a different test from Castorina where reasonable suspicion exists.
legal_issues: Whether opportunity alone provides reasonable grounds for suspicion under Castorina
Whether blanket arrest of six suspects was Wednesbury unreasonable
Whether police should have used voluntary interview given good character and cooperation
Effect of Article 5 ECHR on exercise of arrest discretion

notes: Complex motor insurance contribution appeal between insurers after disputed policy avoidance.

enrichment.short_title: Insurer entitled to equitable contribution after co-insurer's ineffective avoidance of motor policy
key_facts: Mrs Kaur injured a third party while driving her husband Dr Singh's car; she was insured under a Drake policy for any car with owner's consent and named on Dr Singh's Provident policy.
Provident purported to avoid Dr Singh's policy for non-disclosure; Drake settled the third party claim and sought 50% equitable contribution from Provident.
Moore-Bick J held Provident's avoidance valid and Drake a volunteer for paying more than its rateable proportion under its policy clause.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Moore-Bick J's judgment on contribution between motor insurers in a double insurance dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Provident not entitled to avoid its policy; Drake not a volunteer; Drake entitled to 50% equitable contribution from Provident.
enrichment.ratio: A purported avoidance of a motor policy is ineffective where subsequent conduct is inconsistent with treating the contract as at an end; where double insurance exists an insurer paying under protest after notifying dispute is not a volunteer precluded from equitable contribution by a rateable proportion clause, particularly when the co-insurer cannot rely on an arbitration award between itself and the insured to defeat contribution.
legal_issues: Whether Provident validly avoided Dr Singh's policy for non-disclosure
Whether waiver or reinstatement prevented avoidance
Whether Drake's rateable proportion clause limited recovery to 50% from Mrs Kaur and barred contribution
Whether Drake was a volunteer disentitled to contribution under Legal & General v Drake principles

notes: Group litigation test case on ACT compensation following Metallgesellschaft; DTA tax credit offset rejected.

enrichment.short_title: EU parent companies' DTA tax credits cannot offset UK subsidiaries' ACT compensation claims
key_facts: Pirelli UK subsidiaries paid Advance Corporation Tax on dividends to Dutch and Italian parent companies because group income elections under ICTA s 247 were limited to UK-resident groups.

Following Metallgesellschaft/Hoechst the Inland Revenue conceded breach of Article 43 but argued Article 10 DTA tax credit payments to parents were countervailing advantages reducing ACT compensation.
ACT paid between July 1995 and April 1999 totalled over £23 million, part later set off against mainstream corporation tax and part remaining as surplus ACT.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal in the lead group litigation order test claim following Park J's judgment on ACT restitution and compensation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Article 10 DTA payments are not countervailing advantages; parents would still have received tax credits even if group income elections had been permitted; withholding tax issue to be referred to CJEC if it becomes material.
enrichment.ratio: Double taxation treaty tax credits conferred on non-resident parents under Article 10 DTAs are exhaustive reliefs unaffected by domestic exclusions such as ICTA s 247(2) from franked investment income; in assessing ACT compensation for breach of freedom of establishment, DTA payments to a foreign parent cannot reduce restitution owed to the paying UK subsidiary because parent and subsidiary are separate persons for that purpose.
legal_issues: Whether parents would have been entitled to Article 10 DTA tax credits if group income elections had been available
Whether DTA payments must be set off against ACT compensation as countervailing advantages
Whether the Pirelli group should be treated as a single economic unit for restitution purposes
Whether ACT was a withholding tax within the Parent and Subsidiary Directive
